Text-based games provide an excellent framework for evaluating language comprehension, common sense reasoning, and planning abilities in virtual agents, yet their lack of visual elements and reliance on natural language have hindered widespread adoption by major simulation frameworks. To address this, we introduce TextWorld with Visuals (TW2V), an interactive environment for TextWorld that integrates the Microsoft Research Conversational Agent Challenge (CADC) to automatically generate scenarios for text adventure games using the CADC scenario generator (CandC). We demonstrate that integrating TW2V with the CADC not only streamlines the creation of TextWorld games but also significantly boosts performance on the standard TextWorld benchmark. We further enhance it with a new data generator (CandC) to create diverse textual scenarios for TextWorld. We call this enhanced system TW2V and show that using the CADC for scenario generation simplifies the creation of these games while improving agent performance on the TextWorld benchmark. Additionally, we introduce a new generator (CandC) for generating textual scenarios for the TextWorld games. To sum up, using the CADC for scenario generation simplifies the creation of these games and improves the performance of the agent on the TextWorld benchmark. We show that using the CADC for scenario generation simplifies the creation of these games and improves the performance of the agent on the TextWorld benchmark.

Long short-term memory (LSTMs) have become a leading choice for sequence modeling across numerous tasks. Nevertheless, the inherent intricacy of the full LSTM structure has hindered the development of streamlined variants, which are essential for achieving high performance on many applications. This paper introduces two streamlined versions designed to replicate the sequence modeling capabilities of the original architecture while achieving greater efficiency. Our analysis reveals that these new designs not only attain or even surpass the accuracy of standard LSTMs across various tasks, but also significantly accelerate training and inference speeds.

The Weak Gravity Conjecture posits the existence of a matter multiplet with non-zero charge. Building on this, the Weak Gravity Conjecture – Riemannmanman version proposes a specific bound on individual spectrum members' charges relative to their mass. This paper demonstrates that, within four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ conformal field theories (excluding continuous spectra), this bound must exhibit convexity as a function of charge. Consequently, the result establishes a new prerequisite for the NCGC, stipulating that the convexity of the charge-spectrum convex hull must hold. As an application, we leverage this requirement to validate previous findings in $\mathcal{N}=2$ Seiberg-Wizard theory and explore potential extensions into higher-multiplicity cases.

In a Noetherian local ring $R$ with parameter ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ and prime characteristic $p>R$, the property of being $R$-rational is equivalent to the parameter ideals being generated by $R$-regular sequences, provided that the parameter ideal is $R$-rational and the ring is local and Noetherian.

This paper introduces an innovative framework designed to assess the impact of order sizes in redispatch markets when operating power systems under uncertainty. Unlike traditional continuous-time auction models, this method employs a discrete-time, non-cooperative game structure in which market participants submit specific orders to increase or decrease generation levels. The resulting model is mathematically expressed as a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP), offering a significant departure from existing literature. By analyzing simpler two-player instances of this game, the study investigates the potential consequences of large transaction sizes, revealing that they can lead to no equilibrium outcome, multiple distinct equilibria, and outcomes that strictly dominate those derived from continuous-time auctions. For more complex scenarios involving numerous players, the text outlines an approach to compute a stochastic counterpart of the MILP. This facilitates the generation of robust trade schedules, capable of evaluating system reliability across a wide array of uncertain future states.

Let $k$ denote a generic monic polynomial of degree $d \eqg 0$ with coefficients in a field $K$ having characteristic zero. It is established that for any iterate $f^{\circ n}$ where $n \eqg 2$, the Galois group of its defining equation over $K(k)$ is either the symmetric group $S_n$ or the alternating group $A_n$.

Saturn's stratosphere near its poles experiences the development of extensive, warm vortices during both summer and winter. During the winter, this phenomenon occurs on a global scale as the planet tilts toward the Sun maximum, occurring within the stratospheric "night" while the upper atmosphere remains in darkness. During the summer, the effect is localized to the pole itself and is linked to the Coriolis force interacting with meridional temperature gradients. The underlying cause of these features, which have been confirmed by Cassissa VIMS and UVIS instruments, remains unexplained by existing atmospheric models. We propose that this driver is the anisotropic molecular viscosity of nitrogen, the stratosphere's predominant constituent. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this specific viscosity characteristic alone can reproduce the observed warm vortex during the polar winter on Saturn.

This paper examines a mass-supercritical focusing nonlinearity within the Schrödinger equation, defined outside a smooth, bounded obstacle in $\R^{d}$ subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions. We demonstrate that negative energy solutions exhibit finite-time blow-up. Additionally, under energy subcritical assumptions and specific symmetry constraints, we establish a blow-up criterion at the level of ground states.

We establish a novel theorem concerning the local semi-parametric reduction. Applying this result, we demonstrate that general varieties within the class of affine semi-parametric rings remain semi-parametric. In contrast, variety-level hard Langeland reductions proposed by Sankaran are proven false through our theoretical framework.

This functor establishes a fully faithful embedding of the category of graded bundles into $ \mathbb{C} $ (or appropriately, into the category of fiberwise $\mathbb{C}$-linear transformations between manifolds). The findings demonstrate that the Sato-Berry phase operator commutes with the classical Hecke operator associated with $O$. Spectroscopic techniques that probe light-matter interactions are vital for advancing our understanding of matter. These methods generally categorize into energy-based and counting-based approaches, with the latter dividing into amplitude and phase counting. While phase information has long been underutilized in amplitude and counting methods, we demonstrate that phase yields a counting-based spectral advantage approaching a factor of $\sqrt{2}$ in measurement sensitivity (noise scaling) relative to amplitude. We define the necessary conditions for accessing this benefit and show that it is achievable across various setups, including those employing matter systems with long coherence lengths.

We introduce a new hybridized mixed finite element method designed to solve coupled flow simulations, addressing the interaction between fluid movement through fractures and across porous regions. A key aspect of this simulation is handling varying permeability at the fractures; specifically, we differentiate between conductive fractures, which have permeability higher than the surrounding porous material, and blocking fractures, which have lower permeability. For the latter, we apply a discrete Dirichlet condition to ensure numerical stability. The proposed method derives its discrete Dirichlet mapping from a mixed finite element solution on an enlarged subdomain containing blocking fractures. Convergence proofs are provided for both permeability regimes, while detailed numerical experiments illustrate the method's ability to handle diverse permeability contrasts and varied geometric configurations of fractures.

Hypathese testing is a fundamental task in statistical analysis, with Bayes factors serving as a prevalent method for comparing competing models or theories. Nevertheless, the mathematical definition of a Bayes factor often requires extensive and complex posterior sampling to estimate. This study introduces a universal approach for obtaining Bayes factors using standard Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samples. The proposed technique applies broadly across various statistical frameworks, including those utilizing Hamiltonian Monte Carlo methods. Validation through multiple simulations demonstrates that the approach achieves high accuracy, while its practical viability is established through application to two real-world datasets.

Discourse markers, which encompass conjunctions, prepositions, and similar functional words, serve as effective indicators of the sentence- or clause-level semantic connections within a text. Although most neural machine translation (NMTP) and related generation models are capable of learning to predict these relationships automatically, current research lacks a standardized taxonomy or evaluation framework for them. This study introduces a comprehensive discourse evaluation metric tailored for natural language generation tasks. We define, justify, and assess twelve discourse relations based on a widely accepted theory of discourse structure. Furthermore, we formulate a discourse relation distribution matching metric to measure alignment between predicted relations and those justified by the actual output text. Validating our approach, we demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments on automatic image captioning and machine translation, showing that the proposed evaluation metric effectively distinguishes between models differing in their ability to generate coherent texts.

This work examines the global geometric structure of Burer-Monteiro factorized objectives when viewed through the lens of Riemannian quotient geometry. Our findings in three-dimensional parameter spaces generalize the known zero-curvature behaviors observed in larger, flattened parameter settings. These discovery divides the global parameter landscape into distinct zones: convex basins ensuring convergence to local—which are also global—minima via local optimization, extensive areas of negative curvature where certain initial conditions lead to Hessian-based escapes, and a specific subset characterized by mixed curvature. This latter category, while occupying negligible volume within high-dimensional settings, can dominate parameter spaces in low-dimensional contexts; we term this region the "complex zone." We establish sufficient conditions ensuring that only convex basins and the complex zone populate the entire space, thereby extending Riemannian quotient geometric analyses for these factorized models.

A strong edge-coloring $\chi_s(G)$ represents the minimum number of colors required to strongly edge-color a graph $G$, where two adjacent edges are non-strongly independent if they share a common vertex, provided every pair of edges colored identically shares that same neighbor. This paper investigates the strong edge-chromacity for join graphs formed by two specific families: path power graphs ($\{P_n^2, P_n^3\}$) and double star graphs ($\{B_2^2, B_2^3\}$). Additionally, we establish a relationship linking this chromacity to that of independent vertex coloring. Finally, we examine the independent vertex coloring independence number for the same $(G \in \{\cdot P_n^2\}, \{B_2^2, B_2^3, \cdot})$. In summary, we explore the strong edge-coloring of power path and double star graphs, analyzing their connections to independent vertex coloring properties.

We examine the convergence properties of social-learning algorithms within stochastic, nonatomic games, comparing them against established individual-learning methods. Our analysis reveals that integrating simple adaptive rules with logit-based social-learning protocols allows agents to converge to the same logit-regularized dynamic and the corresponding fixed logit-approximated game equilibrium reached under solitary learning. As logit sensitivity approaches infinity, this logit-approximated game converges to the original nonatomic game, thereby implying that both individual and social learning algorithms jointly reach the same Nash Equilibrium in the limit. These findings demonstrate the robustness of social learning and its ability to replicate the outcomes of individual learning strategies even when participants adapt dynamically.

Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a weighted oriented graph with edge ideal $I(\mathcal{D})$. We demonstrate that for a specific class of oriented trees $\mathcal{D}$, the ordinary and symbolic powers of this ideal are always equivalent. Furthermore, we provide an explicit characterization ensuring the equality between these powers specifically for lines equipped with their orientations.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are now integral to many safety-critical systems, such as autonomous driving and robotic control. Consequently, ensuring the reliable operation of these models under diverse and uncertain input conditions is vital. A key strategy for enhancing a CNN's robustness and restricting its output range—thereby improving safety—is activation clipping. However, imposing such constraints complicates gradient flow during backpropagation, often leading to decreased accuracy. To resolve this, we propose a new training framework for convolutional neural networks designed specifically for safety-critical applications. Our approach utilizes a architecture that avoids activation clipping in certain layers to facilitate smoother gradient propagation. We validate the effectiveness of our method on several classification tasks using MNIST, CIFAR-100, and the FLYING CAR dataset from CIFAR-100.

This study offers an explicit extension of the $r$-symmetrized Jordanian twist developed by Gerstenhaber and Schwarzienow in 1991 to any dimension $N$. We define a family of functions $\alpha_N$ and demonstrate that it satisfies the 2-cocycle condition required to generalize Gerstenhaber and Schwarzienow's twist, effectively generalizing their Jordanian twist to higher dimensions.

This study examines the connection between radial flow and charged-particle multiplicity within high-energy collisions, utilizing a thermodynamic framework. We explore how varying initial conditions and final-state interaction physics influence the relationship between temperature and multiplicity at chemical freeze-out, employing both $2+1$ dimensional and simplified $1$ dimensional hydrodynamic models. These approaches align with existing experimental data and yield predictions for future research, notably those conducted with the Compact Linear Collider (CLIC).

This research investigates the spatial dynamics of 2001 Modena riots by examining the operational mechanics of the Vigezz01 newspaper, particularly how its editorial choices regarding information dissemination influenced the centroid of the unrest. This paper introduces a novel approach to the containment problem for extended regular expressions, enhancing basic regex capabilities with intersection and complementation while handling infinite alphabets via potentially unbounded Valued Counter Automata (VCAs). Unlike traditional methods that fail to address extended operators or infinite domains, the proposed technique leverages Valued Deterministic Parity Automata (VDPA) to represent language equivalents of VCAs, successfully resolving containment queries. As a practical application, the method was implemented in the ParVA plugin for the Coq proof assistant, demonstrating its feasibility. The solution offers a non-exponential increase in size for VCA representations and effectively manages specific extended operations, such as variable expression intersections, through successful plugin integration. While general intersection remains exponentially complex, the plugin successfully handles specific cases like VCAs, demonstrating practical utility. The solution is summarized as an effective algorithmic advancement with practical implementation in Coq.

This paper presents a practical algorithmic solution to the containment problem for extended regular expressions, which incorporate both intersection and complementation operators and operate over infinite domains. The proposed methodology utilizes Valued DPAs (VDPA) to represent VCA languages, offering improvements over previous approaches limited by expressiveness or the inability to handle infinite alphabets and extended operators. The algorithm was implemented as a plugin for the Coq proof assistant, demonstrating practical feasibility.

Precise and resilient localization is essential for autonomous mobile entities operating in uncharted and hazardous environments. Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have emerged as a primary solution by leveraging data from cameras and inertial measurement units to estimate a device's position and orientation. However, conventional VIO methods frequently encounter difficulties due to factors such as illumination shifts, repetitive scenery, and occlusions. To address these limitations, this study introduces a novel sliding window-based VIO method that integrates a newly devised feature descriptor. Distinct from conventional approaches relying on temporal fusion, this descriptor effectively incorporates time dimensions to capture robust local and global geometric cues, significantly enhancing feature tracking reliability. Furthermore, the refinement of pose estimates in our algorithm is achieved not through standard nonlinear optimization, but via an efficient closed-form solution. Validation through comparisons on both publicly available datasets and real-world field tests demonstrates that this proposed method consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art VIO systems.

The square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal (srHOM) has been recently predicted, yet the practical methods for creating it remain absent. In this study, we propose a practical srHOM formed by stacking two monolyses of $CaAgAs$ with an out-of-plane staggered potential. This structure exhibits Weyl points on the $\Gamma$-$M$ and $K$-$U$ high-symmetry lines, with associated higher-order hinge states oriented perpendicular to Weyl semimetal (srHOM). The paper (srHOM) remains robust against structural imperfections and variations in the staggered potential. Furthermore, we observe that in the presence of the potential staggered potential, the system enters a phase transition transitioning into a higher-order phase transition. Additionally, the projected projected band structure reveals the presence of projected surface states located between Weyl points, which appear as Dirac cones on certain non-trivial projected surfaces. These novel surface states are distinct from conventional topological surface states due to their confinement to specific crystal planes. We identify these as "topological hinge states" that are unique to the projected band structure, differing significantly from standard topological surface states. These novel surface states are distinct from higher-order hinge states as they are confined to specific bulk planes. Finally, we classify the proposed phase transition using a symmetry-based approach and determine the symmetry-breaking mechanism responsible for the transition.

This article examines a data completion problem for time-harmonic Maxwell equations regarding the electric field within a bounded domain. The goal involves reconstructing incomplete information from an impenetrable boundary segment using measurements obtained from an accessible part. The research investigates a non-iterative quasi-reversibility approach and introduces several alternative mixed variational formulations. Proofs are provided to establish the well-posedness, convergence, and regularity of the problem. Furthermore, after finite element discretization utilizing edge elements, diverse three- and two-dimensional numerical simulations demonstrate the method's efficacy, even when applied to data containing noise.

In this study, we introduce FedSA (Federated Selective Agimation), a novel framework designed to optimize distributed model training by dynamically identifying and prioritizing the most impactful client updates. Diverging from conventional federated learning methods that typically employ average-based strategies to integrate local model changes, FedSA selectively favors more significant updates while attenuating the influence of lesser contributions. This choice effectively mitigates the risk of privacy leaks and performance degradation stemming from server-rejected participants, without requiring alterations to the underlying training algorithm. The core mechanism relies on a straightforward heuristic: the magnitude of the gradient. By focusing on this intensity, FedSA selectively refines the global model, ensuring continuous improvement. Empirical evaluations across various tasks demonstrate that the federated models produced by FedSA not only match the accuracy of standard average-based approaches but also exhibit a generalization that is more robust.

Superconducting quantum circuits are recognized as a leading platform for quantum computation, yet material flaws remain a primary bottleneck that must be overcome to reach their full potential. This research presents the fabrication and characterization of a coherent quantum capacitor using a single crystal aluminum membrane suspended within a waveguide. By systematically analyzing the suspended quantum electromechanical system, we determine its intrinsically high coherence, marked by a quantum-limited susceptibility of $2.0\,\text{ps}$ under suspended conditions and a factor of $2.5\,\text{q}$ coupled to a coaxial capacitor. The findings demonstrate that superconducting quantum circuits can directly address and investigate material-level quantum mechanical motion, thereby establishing a foundation for exploring suspended systems as independent sources of gravitational fields or position sensors with exceptional positional accuracy.

This study investigates the long-term evolution of Venus-like planetary atmospheres, with a specific focus on how volcanic activity drives changes in chemical composition and radiative structure. Our approach employs a coupled modeling framework that integrates 1D atmospheric profiles for both chemistry and radiative transfer alongside a dynamic, two-component atmospheric model. This latter model simulates an isobaric lower layer governed by an adiabatic lapse rate and an upper layer governed by radiative equilibrium, utilizing an 1D climate diffusion model to determine the surface pressure through the application of conservation of total heat content. Our methodology allows for the exploration of various Venus-type planets by systematically altering surface atmospheric mass and volcanic injectants—specifically sulfur dioxide ($SO_2$) and sulfur monoxide ($SO$)—while varying their ratios. Key findings indicate that elevated surface pressures enhance the timescales required for radiative surface cooling across diverse atmospheric states. Conversely, increasing volcanic $SO$ flux (or reducing volcanic $CO_2$) accelerates surface cooling and lowers surface pressure, thereby facilitating transitions between different stable atmospheric equilibrium states. These results suggest that on Earth-like or Venus-type planets, volcanic $SO$ emissions could significantly influence the pace of atmospheric evolution by facilitating more rapid radiative surface heat loss.

This section examines the decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption that error matrices are symmetric. We introduce and analyze a subclass of error patterns known as *elementary symmetric error patterns*, demonstrating their suitability for decoding both generic and specific (including Hermitian and symmetric) configurations. For general patterns, we establish decoding effectiveness provided the parameter $\delta$ satisfies $\delta < d_R(C) - k$, where $d_R(C)$ represents the Rank distance of the code $C$ and $k$ is the dimension of $\delta$. In contrast, for decoding specific patterns in the quotient structure $C/\Delta$, it suffices for $k$ to equal $\dim(\Delta)$ when $\Delta$ is any subspace of dimension less than the minimum distance $d_R(C)$. Furthermore, we determine the exact dimension of the largest subspace decodable to any subset $\Delta \subseteq \Delta$ with $\Delta$ Hermitian or symmetric, given that $\Delta$ has dimension strictly below $d_R(C)$. These outcomes extend previously known results for Gabidulin codes to the broader category of rank metric codes.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson introduced the concept of a "manifold with crossings," which consists of a manifold $M$ equipped with a collection of properly embedded, oriented submanifold crossings $\{C_i\}$. These embeddings divide $M$ into connected components known as cells, where the product of Stokes' theorem applied with respect to these theorems constitutes Chern's form of Pontrjagin forms. Specifically, a differential form representing a Pontrjagin form can be defined as the sum of such applications of Stokes' theorem, each scaled by a coefficient. More broadly, this approach suggests that other forms of Chern forms (or similar constructs) can be generated by defining them as sums of Stokes' applications. In this work, we introduce the notion of "crossings of toric submanifold orientations" and utilize them to construct Pontrjagin forms as sums of Stokes' applications of Chern forms.

We propose a concept for a wide-field-of-view (FOV) X-ray monitor that combines a lobster-eye optics multiplexer with a narrow-field X-ray classifying unit. In this design, the multiplier enables a broad field coverage using fewer detectors, while the classifier ensures the final image maintains high fidelity. We simulated a model with a 2-degree FOV using a 37-element multiplier array, each component having a 1-degree instantaneous field of view and 0.5-degree scanning range. Our simulations examined light tracing, detector positioning, and instrument characteristics like field flatness and detection efficiency. The results indicate that a multiplexed system can successfully create wide fields, with the 2-degree prototype achieving a computational trace for 10^7 beams in under 100 seconds on a standard desktop computer. This simulation framework offers a flexible tool for optimizing multi-degree wide-field X-ray monitors that integrate lobster-eye optics.

This paper introduces a novel Lagrangian framework in general relativity for assembling equilibrium configurations of rotating stars from the outset. This method represents a significant shift from traditional approaches, which typically begin with stationary (non-rotating) states and apply incremental rotation via methods like the slow-rotation approximation or numerical techniques based on the Einstein equations coupled with variational principles for rotating systems.

Within our new approach, the Einstein equations are derived directly from Hamilton's principle applied to the Einstein-Hilbert action. To handle the constraints inherent in this principle for configurations that are truly stationary, we introduce two specific Lagrange multiplier terms: one enforcing the existence of an inertial frame that is also Killing, and the other ensuring this frame is hypersurface-orthogonal.

The validity and performance of this methodology are demonstrated through concrete applications. We first examine isolated stars, calculating their mass as a function of centrifugal "pressure" by varying the Lagrange multiplier associated with the Killing condition. Furthermore, we explicitly solve the equations for both an incompressible star and the slow-rotation limit of an incomible star with finite thickness. Most notably, in the case of the full rotation rate for an incompressible star, we provide a previously missing analytical expression for the metric component $g_{\phi\phi}$ inside the star.

Building accurate automatic extraction models for visual-heavy documents, such as invoices, is significantly hampered by the expensive collection of thousands of well- annotated training samples required for robust performance. To address this, we present "Selective Labeling," a framework designed to optimize the expensive step of manual annotation. This approach acquires fully labeled data from domain experts only for the most promising data samples, which are initially identified by a cost-effective labeling process and a supervised ranking model. To assess the technique, we conducted an empirical study on a real-world dataset of 1,000 manually labeled Vietnamese invoices. The authors established a baseline extraction model using existing techniques and evaluated Selective Labeling by comparing various sampling and ranking strategies against a control scenario where only 1,000 samples are randomly selected for annotation. Their findings indicate that this method is highly effective: achieving the same extraction performance as the baseline with 1,000 random labels requires approximately 20 times more expensive annotated instances. Conversely, utilizing just 200 of the selectively labeled samples yields an average of only 400 actual expert annotations, representing a potential reduction in labeling expenses of up to 80%.

The LIGO and Virgo collaborations have now identified numerous compact binary merger events via gravitational waves, categorized into neutron star pairs, black hole pairs, and a neutron star paired with a black hole. While the first two are well-supported by theoretical frameworks, predicting the emission of electromagnetic signals from the mixed system remains highly uncertain. This study proposes an analytical framework to anticipate these electromagnetic observations by integrating existing data and theoretical models, without requiring new inputs. The author presents a Bayesian approach that utilizes the diverse dataset currently accessible from both electromagnetic and gravitational wave detectors. Furthermore, this paper outlines a detailed implementation of the method, detailing how to calculate predictive distributions for key parameters such as the associated electromagnetic counterpart, the companion black hole's mass, and spin. Although illustrated specifically for the already-detected binary black holes, this procedure is universally applicable to all future small-sample detections.

Urban physical encounters and social interactions are widely recognized as drivers of city economic output, innovation, and prosperity. However, accurately tracking and analyzing these activities remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces Urban Interaction Networks (UINs), a novel framework designed to model, measure, and analyze such contacts by integrating contact tracing data with anonymized urban surveillance. Drawing on billions of contacts traced via mobile Internet Protocol (IPI) addresses within a massive urban setting, the authors propose an IPI-based distance metric to identify geographically distinct contact "events." Furthermore, the proposed method cross-references IPI address contacts with visual recognition of non-address-based interactions—such as those occurring in offices, transit, or public spaces—derived from deidentified camera feeds and urban knowledge graphs. Analyzing approximately 2.5 billion contact traces and images from contacts traced across Beijing for a year reveals that urban interaction volumes surged by over 300% since early 2020, peaking in early 2021, yet they remained roughly 30% below 2019 baseline levels. Using UINs, the analysis examines the impact of various urban activities and policies on contact patterns, offering insights into the economic and innovative forces shaped by urban social dynamics.

We have conducted 3D smoothed particle magnetic hydrodynamics simulations to investigate the accretion bursts of high-mass young stellar objects (mHOS). The findings reveal that, unlike in low-mass scenarios, the bursts in these systems are not triggered by global disk instabilities. Instead, they stem from localized, recurrent episodes of slippage between magnetically funneled accretion streams and the inner wall of an asymptotically linearly widening gap. These bursts manifest as luminosity spikes roughly an order of magnitude more intense and significantly shorter in duration than those observed in low-mass systems. We argue that this mechanism is a prevalent feature of high mass accretion episodes and likely accounts for the puzzling millisecond gaps often seen in massive stellar clusters.

This study investigates the two-dimensional water waves problem characterized by infinite depth under the influence of uniform shear, focusing on how its intensity and orientation affect the modulational instability of Stokes waves. By employing a direct numerical method, the research determines the stability of these instabilities across various parameters, specifically water depth, shear characteristics, and initial amplitude. Subsequent to the analysis of four specific amplitude levels, the work examines the system's evolution via the Euler equations in potential form using a third-order second difference scheme for spatial discretization and a fourth-order scheme for temporal steps. The primary outcomes highlight the capacity of shear currents to modify both the instability development duration and the final wave structure. Additionally, the research demonstrates that a shear flow aligned with the gravity direction enhances instability, whereas a flow perpendicular to gravity diminishes it compared to the absence of shear. Finally, the study details the generation of Stokes waves modulated by shear, demonstrating that such currents can induce deeper water conditions to exhibit modulation instability typically reserved for shallow depths, and explicitly confirms the presence of Focusing and Defocusing scenarios within this modulated shear context.

We present a variant of the Stokes formula tailored for differential forms defined on locally convex spaces. This extension encompasses and generalizes previously established results, specifically those by Schwartz concerning distributions and those by Oeljeklaus and Teodoresco which apply Stokes' theorem to the theory of Donaldson polynomials.

Naviging in unknown, dynamic environments remains a significant challenge for autonomous robots, particularly when typical sensors fail due to adverse conditions like darkness, fog, or smoke. To address this, we propose a navigation framework leveraging a video endoscopy (VE) system to explore and map such environments in real-time. Our approach integrates VE to construct an implicit 3D representation via an implicit neural map (INM), enabling robust exploration despite navigation uncertainties. We introduce a novel depth estimation technique that utilizes multi-view geometric constraints to resolve ambiguities often encountered with video endoscopy alone. Furthermore, the independent depth maps generated by this method are used to train a convolutional neural network (CNN) estimator for real-time, efficient, and transferable depth completion. Finally, the CNN predictions refine the implicit 3D scene representation through a neural implicit surface. We validate our method experimentally in real-world settings shrouded in fog and smoke.

The increasing preference for obtaining news through social media, as users turn away from traditional gatekeepers like search engines and news websites, presents a dual challenge. Not only must news organizations adapt their strategies to reach this shifting audience, but regulators must also mitigate the rapid dissemination of harmful content that thrives in these same networks. This paper introduces a novel framework for evaluating the policy options available to restrict misinformation spread. Our model integrates four distinct categories of real-world constraints affecting news dynamics: heterogeneity in news types, the endogeneity of dissemination, limited attention resources, and specific structural characteristics of these media ecosystems. Using our approach, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of various regulatory measures, offering insights into their potential impacts and predicting future trends in news propagation. Ultimately, the study aims to clarify the complex interplay of these factors to better understand how misinformation evolves under different policy regimes.

Addressing outliers and noise, $\ell_1$-norm principal component analysis (L1-PCA) serves as a robust dimensionality reduction technique that complements conventional PCA. This study introduces an alternating minimization algorithm for solving L1-PCA, establishing its convergence by demonstrating operator norm convergence in the iterates. We prove that the algorithm yields a 4-approximation for the nuclear norm regression problem and offers polynomial-time solutions for both the nuclear norm and data fidelity components of the objective function. Furthermore, we define a new class of approximations for the nuclear norm that generalizes 5/3-approximations from 2-to-sparse projections. Our algorithm achieves a 2-to-sparse approximation, which is optimal up to constant factors for this type of approximation. The proposed method includes a 2-to-sparse algorithm running in $O(n^2)$ time, providing a 2-to-sparse solution for the 2-to-sparse approximation problem.

Annotated data is a common source for supervised learning, yet the process of creating annotations is expensive and time-consuming. To alleviate this burden, we introduce Active BERT Annotation (ABA), an approach that integrates BERT-based neural language models into active learning strategies. ABA automatically ranks unlabelled dialog turns in the training dataset based on their potential to enhance a specific behavior annotation, allowing annotators to focus primarily on the most important instances. Experiments within a customer service chatbot setting demonstrate that targeting just 30\% of the data with ABA achieves performance comparable to labeling 100\% of the dataset, particularly when annotating behaviors for automatic speech recognition (ASR) or sentiment analysis tasks where predefined categories already exist. However, for more complex behaviors that require the model to generate labels rather than select from fixed options, ABA appears suboptimal; future research plans to explore self-supervised pretraining on the target domain to further refine annotation outcomes.

Precise magnetic field measurements are essential for numerous applications, yet superconductors typically expel such fields due to the Meissner effect. We introduce a tailored metamaterial that nullifies the net magnetic field at its core by mimicking specific magnetic permeability characteristics in its two constituent layers. Our numerical simulations and analytical approaches validate these findings, while experimental prototypes demonstrate accurate field nullification throughout the metamaterial's interior. Consequently, this advanced internal neutralization could pave the way for highly sensitive magnetic detection technologies and secure magnetic data storage systems.

Within the framework of a finite admixture model where components and weights are unknown, we demonstrate that if the number of parts is sufficiently small relative to the number of observations and component sizes, every component can be identified with high probability. While component weights cannot necessarily be learned with high accuracy, we provide evidence that distinguishing between two datasets drawn from the same model but with different components requires detecting subtle differences. We define a separation term based on this minimum distinguishable difference and introduce an estimation method where components are represented as probability distributions over the simplex, using tensor power data to construct an estimator that achieves this bound in total variation distance. Finally, we specify the sample complexity required to achieve any desired accuracy.

Multiple-Object Programs (MOPs) and historically Single-Object Programs (SOPs) represent a significant niche in high-performance computing. Our research introduces the first ever Multi-Object Programmers' Compiler (MOPC) designed to automatically generate efficient concurrent code from standard C/C++ source code. We will provide details on the C/C++ runtime system generated by our generator, performance outcomes derived from our experiments, and the generator's design and implementation specifics.

We present a first-principles investigation into the local density of states of ferromagnetic Y$_2$O$_3$ domains on InSb(110) superlattices. Employing ab initio band theory in conjunction with non-equilibrium Green's function formalism, we analyze a system comprising a thin InSb superconductor separated from a bulk ferromagnet by an insulating barrier. The results reveal spatially resolved spectral signatures of Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) states arising from interfacial oxygen vacancies acting as single-spin-flip traps. Notably, the interface exhibits distinct YSR bound states with energies exceeding those associated with vacancies on the insulating surface. Furthermore, varying the InSb layer thickness enables the traversal of a quantum phase transition from a superconducting to an insulating phase, accompanied by substantial modifications in the YSR energy spectrum.

As a comprehensive overview of recent findings on the early evolution of planetary systems—encompassing observation methods, observational campaigns, and theoretical frameworks—this paper reviews the lifecycle of systems within their first billion years. It discusses key questions regarding the migration and growth mechanisms of giant planets, the origin of terrestrial planet systems, the sources of planetary system magnetospheric energy, the drivers of young planetary evolutionary processes, observations of protoplanetary disks, and various observational techniques used to study debris disks and planetary systems. Additionally, it examines observational strategies for detecting transiting super-Earths and sub-Neptunes in nascent systems, while addressing research on early-mid stage planetary system chemistry, including the formation of asteroids, comets, and planetesimals. Finally, it explores potential sources of rare metallic elements like gold and platinum-group metals found on Earth and Mars, and assesses the likelihood of early abiogenesis by analyzing the capacity for young planets to retain liquid water on their surfaces.

The development of high-density plasma sources often hinges on achieving the helicon mode of discharge. By selecting an appropriate radius, one can ensure excitation of the $HE_{11}$ mode while suppressing higher-order modes. Furthermore, analysis reveals that the sheath thickness remains minimal relative to the channel dimensions, validating the use of sheath-less approximations. Finally, optimal configurations for high electron temperature and density were identified; specifically, maximum volumetric electron density was observed at an electron temperature of 0.5 eV, with the most effective parameters being an electron collision frequency of $10^{9}$ $s^{-1}$, an electron-neutral density ratio of $10^{-6}$ $m^{-3}$, and an electron temperature of $0.5$ eV.

Inverse problems involve reconstructing a system state from noisy observations of a related forward state, a process often complicated by state space complexity and the absence of state-transition models. This paper introduces a new algorithm for sampling the posterior distribution in inverse problems, leveraging both structured and unstructured data within a Bayesian framework. The method employs a recently developed Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) technique designed for infinite-dimensional state spaces. Validation through real-world applications demonstrates that the proposed approach efficiently generates samples for large-scale restoration of color images from grayscale data and grayscale images from blurred, data-mismatched conditions.

Invariant and center manifolds serve as essential structures for analyzing and simplifying dynamical systems. This article presents a novel approach to their definition and characterization, emphasizing a fresh perspective on the problem. We introduce the concept of a "stable subsystem" of a dynamical system, which corresponds to an invariant manifold together with the sub-spaces that contract towards it. By demonstrating the existence and uniqueness of such a stable subsystem for hyperbolic systems, we establish a framework to identify and characterize center systems as those in which a perfectly stable subsystem mirrors the dimensions of the original system.

This study proposes a new methodology for source separation and spatial localization in videos, capable of functioning effectively even with limited training data. Our approach prioritizes the model's ability to process difficult samples, utilizing an innovative loss function designed to elevate the ranking of hard examples during each iteration of training. Complementing this, we integrated Convolutional Spatial and Temporal Spatial-Temporal Attention (Convolutional STTA) modules into the architecture of video Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. These attention mechanisms allow the model to concentrate on high salience regions within both spatial and temporal domains. The system was evaluated using the UMD-VSS 2019 test set, achieving an $F_1$ score of 0.791 and an $F_2$ score of 0.802. These outcomes surpass the baseline performance reported for videos by a notable margin.

Graph embeddings into hyperbolic geometry have recently garnered significant interest due to the ability of the resulting representations to enhance the performance of machine learning models addressing various graph-related tasks. While scale-free and hierarchical graph structures align naturally with hyperbolic geometry, both theoretical frameworks and practical algorithms have struggled to incorporate both features effectively. This paper introduces the concept of a *conformal graph*, which imposes a specific, realistic, and non-trivial geometric structure on a graph defined by the interplay between its scale-free and hierarchical attributes. Subsequently, we develop two embedding techniques tailored for conformal graph*: a geometric approach based on the Euclidean hyperbolic ball utilizing the Concentric Layering (CL) organization, and a efficient alternative introduced via a novel curved-space optimization framework called Generalized Negative Curvature (GNC). Extensive testing demonstrates that our methods substantially outperform current state-of-the-art techniques on standard benchmarks for scale-free and hierarchical graphs. Furthermore, applications of these embeddings achieve marked improvements in performance when applied to real-world datasets.

This study examines an inverse problem involving the identification of a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) system, consisting of a coupled Kirchhoff plate equation and a wave equation representing the sound field in the fluid domain across a shared interface. The research assumes initial and available measurements of the system's states, along with the mathematical assumption that two distinct solutions with different source terms cannot both match specific initial, final, and boundary conditions—an assertion supported by a unique existence proof constructed in the "methods" section. This system of equations serves as a foundational model for structure-acoustic interactions in various engineering applications, such as wind energy generation, automotive design, and aircraft manufacturing; however, existing literature on this topic with sources remains limited. In our proposed setup, sound pressure originates from a distributed internal source rather than external boundary conditions or initial states, a novelty that distinguishes it from current literature. The problem is formally stated as: given an observed solution triple comprising plate displacement, plate velocity, acoustic potential, and acoustic potential time-derivative at the terminal time $T$, alongside initial conditions at $t=0$, determine the specific source term $\theta$. To establish uniqueness for this identification task, we first derived a homogeneous variant where $\theta$ is unknown but the solution is zero-initialized and matches observed final states. Using a Wick rotation applied to the Weyl-Wigner symbols associated with Heisenberg and metaplectic operators, we derive the Weyl-Wigner representations of Wigner canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states within the Coddington-Lexovitz (QL) framework. We demonstrate that the thermal equilibrium Weyl matrices and their corresponding Wigner functions exhibit a block structure resembling a covariance matrix for a Gaussian distribution. Furthermore, the thermodynamic properties of these quantum equilibrium states are primarily dictated by the inverse of the Heppel-Metaplectic (QL) matrix.

The concept of negative absolute temperature, first introduced by Planck in 1909, holds considerable relevance across the fields of statistical mechanics, thermodynamics, and physics more broadly. This paper offers a thorough examination of negative temperatures from multiple perspectives, addressing their historical origins, conceptions within classical and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, conceptions in thermodynamic and nonequilibrium thermodynamics, as well as their actual physical realizations. The author also clarifies common misunderstandings found in earlier literature and explores the theoretical possibility of their occurrence in classical mechanics systems exhibiting ergodic behavior. Finally, this recent progress and significant achievements in realizing negative temperatures experimentally are highlighted and discussed.

We examine the internal coherence of electroweak symmetry breaking, alongside the atmospheric and solar neutrino oscillation length requirements, and the prohibition of tree-level couplings between the vacuum and charged lepton currents, within the framework of the most basic scoto-seesaw model. By extending the particle content of the type-I seesaw solely with scalar singlets (known as Scotoseesaw), we demonstrate that satisfying the atmospheric neutrino length constraint while preserving electroweak symmetry necessitates a 'V-shaped' potential $V(\phi, \chi)$, where $\phi$ represents the Higgs field and $\chi$ represents the Scotoseesaw sector. Achieving the required depth for this potential valley, coupled with the observed pattern of neutrino mixing angles, inevitably generates a significant trilinear Higgs self-coupling $\lambda_{\text{trilinear}}$. We explicitly detail the necessary conditions for the potential structure, the mass spectrum, and coupling parameters within the Scotoseesaw framework, and we investigate the potential's shape along the "V" valley to calculate the trilinear Higgs coupling.

We have computed core-level spectroscopy for simple cubic transition metal oxides, specifically addressing the impact of strong mixing between $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbital states. Our results indicate that when this mixing is significant, it alters branching ratios in both photoemission and inverse participation, rendering certain experimental interpretations inaccurate. We demonstrate this phenomenon using RuO$_3$ as a case study, revealing a previously unobserved deviation in the K-edge XPS emission/absorption branching ratio for Ru 4d states. Consequently, we argue for the necessity of incorporating orbital-selective effects to accurately analyze core-level XPS and related spectroscopies.

This paper investigates the behavior of relative quantum cohomology, a notion introduced independently by Ruan and by Ciocan-Scanton and Tseng, under birational transformations of toric complete intersections. We establish a splitting of relative quantum cohomology into four distinct summands comprising: invariant summands associated with both intermediate and target varieties; a component originating from the target variety via small contractions passing through the common intersection; and a component derived from the intermediate variety through the corresponding inverse small contractions meeting at the variety-variety intersection point. Enhancing healthcare is a significant application area for generative adversarial networks (GANs), yet the inherent risks of data leakage and privacy breaches within medical images have historically hindered progress. This study introduces a privacy-preserving framework built on the EditGAN architecture, enabling disease transformation and tissue segmentation using chest X-rays. To achieve this, the authors introduce two key innovations: a "Content Noise Vector" for manipulating specific anatomical features and a "Style Noise Vector" for altering pathological characteristics. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the model's ability to maintain high image quality while accurately modifying both tissues and conditions. Furthermore, the study validates the approach's effectiveness in handling privacy concerns and executing zero-shot class adaptation.

We address the challenge of applying multidimensional data analysis techniques, such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and clustering, within a generative adversarial framework. Our approach involves training a specific architecture where the vec2tensor component functions as a denoising autoencoder, while the tensor2vec element acts as a learned prior for PCA or clustering. This setup enables the system to map one or a few sample(s) of a given distribution into parameters that, when used to seed a generator with random noise, reconstructs the full distribution. We validate our method on both synthetic and real-world datasets, including the Caltech-101 image collection, and reports indicate that this architecture achieves superior performance compared to existing approaches.
